etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English fole (“fool”), from Old French fol (cf. modern French fou (“mad”)) from Latin follis. Doublet of follis and folly. Displaced native Old English dwæs.

definitions.definition: (derogatory) A person with poor judgment or little intelligence.

quote.citation: a. 1569 (date written), Roger Ascham, edited by Margaret Ascham, The Scholemaster: Or Plaine and Perfite Way of Teaching Children, to Vnderstand, Write, and Speake, the Latin Tong, […], London:  […]  John Daye, […], published 1570, →OCLC:
quote.text: Erasmus, [...] saide wiselie that experience is the common scholehouse of foles, and ill men: Men of witte and honestie, be otherwise instructed.

quote.citation: 1748, [Samuel Richardson], “Letter LII”, in Clarissa. Or, The History of a Young Lady: […], volume IV, London:  […]  S[amuel] Richardson;  […], →OCLC:
quote.text: No man is always a fool, every man is sometimes.

quote.citation: 1841 February–November, Charles Dickens, “Barnaby Rudge. Chapter 13.”, in Master Humphrey’s Clock, volume III, London: Chapman & Hall, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: 'If I coloured at all, Mr Edward,' said Joe, 'which I didn't know I did, it was to think I should have been such a fool as ever to have any hope of her. She’s as far out of my reach as—as Heaven is.'

quote.citation: 1895, Rudyard Kipling, If—:
quote.text: If you can bear to hear the truth you've spoken⁠Twisted by knaves to make a trap for fools

quote.citation: 2001, Starsailor (lyrics and music), “Poor Misguided Fool”:
quote.text: You're just a poor misguided foolWho thinks they know what I should doA line for me and a line for youI lose my right to a point of view.

quote.citation: 2008, Adele, Crazy for You:
quote.text: And every time I'm meant to be acting sensibleYou drift into my headAnd turn me into a crumbling fool.

quote.citation: 2017 April 13, Mitchy Collins, Samantha Derosa, Christian Medice, “Broken”, in Finding It Hard to Smile‎[1], performed by Lovelytheband:
quote.text: I like that you're brokenBroken like meMaybe that makes me a fool

definitions.definition: (historical) A jester; a person whose role was to entertain a sovereign and the court (or lower personages).

quote.citation: 1896, Frederick Peterson IN Popular Science Monthly Volume 50 December 1896 , Idiots Savants
quote.text: This court fool could say bright things on occasion, but his main use to the ladies and lords of the palace was to serve as victim to practical jokes, cruel, coarse, and vulgar enough to be appreciated perhaps in the Bowery.

definitions.definition: (literature) A stock character typified by unintelligence, naïveté or lucklessness, usually as a form of comic relief; often used as a source of insight or pathos for the audience, as such characters are generally less bound by social expectations.
Someone who has been made a fool of or tricked; dupe.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto IV:
quote.text: Such clouds of nameless trouble cross⁠All night below the darken’d eyes;⁠With morning wakes the will, and cries,‘Thou shalt not be the fool of loss.’

definitions.definition: (informal) Someone who derives pleasure from something specified.

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “Samson Agonistes, […]”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Can they think me  […]  their fool or jester?

quote.citation: 1975, Foghat, "Fool for the City" (song), Fool for the City (album):
quote.text: I'm a fool for the city.

definitions.definition: (slang, chiefly African-American Vernacular, Hispanic) An informal greeting akin to buddy, dude, or man.

quote.citation: 2010, G.C. Deuce, From the Gutter to the Grave: An American Hood Novel, Xlibris Corporation, →ISBN, page 291:
quote.text: Upon opening the door, Trech was suddenly drawn aback by the  shocking presence of the armed goon standing directly in front of him. “Yo, what  up fool?  […] ”

quote.citation: 2012, Peron Long, Livin' Ain't Easy, Urban Books, →ISBN:
quote.text: “What up, fool?” he finally responded. “Not too much; fell asleep watching your  boys get their asses kicked,” I told him, referring to the Carolina Cougars, the last  team he played for before he got sick.

quote.citation: 2014, Hitta Lo, Bracing Season I, Kaleidoscopic Publishing, →ISBN:
quote.text: Fame leaves out the house and walks to the BP gas station on Alabama Avenue.  On the way there he sees his man Mark posted up at the rec center and walks over to holla at him. “What’s up fool?” Mark says while dapping Fame up.

quote.citation: 2018, Keith L. Bell, Drought Season Over: The Sequel, Xlibris Corporation, →ISBN:
quote.text: “What up fool?” Lil Slim said noticing the seriousness in Lil Kilo’s voice. “You ain’t  switched up on us have you.” Lil Fresh looked at Lil Kilo like where that come  from. “Nigga I’ll neva switch up.” Lil Slim said feeling a little offended.

definitions.definition: (tarot, often capitalized Fool) A particular card in a tarot deck, representing a jester.

quote.citation: 1918, Florence White Williams, The Little Red Hen:
quote.text: She bit it gently and found that it resembled a worm in no way whatsoever as to taste although because it was long and slender, a Little Red Hen might easily be fooled by its appearance.

quote.citation: 1986 June 6, Richard Feynman, “Personal observations on the reliability of the Shuttle”, in Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, Report to the President:
quote.text: There appears to be no process of gradually fooling oneself while degrading standards so characteristic of the Solid Rocket Booster or Space Shuttle Main Engine safety systems.

quote.citation: 2008, BioWare, Mass Effect (Science Fiction), Redwood City: Electronic Arts, →ISBN, →OCLC, PC, scene: Noveria:
quote.text: Liara: Do not be fooled by these civilized surroundings. This is a place of secrets and lies.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To act in an idiotic manner; to act foolishly.

quote.citation: 1681/1682, John Dryden, The Spanish Fryar
quote.text: Is this a time for fooling?

quote.citation: 1972, Judy Blume, Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing, page 56:
quote.text: She's always complaining that she got stuck with the worst possible committee. And that me and Jimmy fool more than we work.

definitions.definition: (archaic) To make a fool of; to make act the fool.

quote.citation: c. 1599 to 1601, William Shakespeare, Hamlet, III.ii.384:
quote.text: They fool me to the top of my bent.

quote.citation: 1909, Gene Stratton-Porter, A Girl of the Limberlost:
quote.text: Of all the fool, fruitless jobs, making anything of a creature that begins by deceiving her, is the foolest a sane woman ever undertook.

quote.citation: 2011, Gayle Kaye, Sheriff Takes a Bride:
quote.text: That was a fool thing to do. You could have gotten yourself shot

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old French fouler (“to mix or mash”).

definitions.definition: (cooking) A type of dessert made of puréed fruit and custard or cream.

quote.citation: 1913, Pearson's Magazine, volume 36, part 2, page 373:
quote.text: Eton is renowned for its "messes," and "strawberry mess" is Empress of them all, with raspberry mess as a very good second. It does not at all convey the joys of a "mess" to say that it consists of iced fruit and cream, and somewhat resembles a "fool." It is a thing apart, and should be approached with bated breath and unimpaired capacity.

quote.citation: 2014, Lindsey Bareham, Just One Pot:
quote.text: Pellaprat [...] invented the dish [of Eton mess] when a load of over-ripe strawberries needed eating up. His disguise was a fluff of whipped cream and the fool was served with sponge fingers. Somewhere along the line, someone else had the idea of stirring chunks of meringue into the fool at the last moment.
